name: Elegy-Pale
geological_features: Vast ice shelves floating on a subsurface ammonia-water ocean
Ice volcanoes erupting mixtures of water and ammonia
Pressure ridges where ice shelves collide, forming jagged walls
specific_features: The Pale Bloom — vast colonies of white-pigmented ice algae that cover the surface in organic carpets
Ammonia hot springs where the subsurface ocean breaches the ice, supporting dense microbial mats
resources: Ammonia-water mixture for rocket propellant manufacturing
Ice algae biomass for nutritional supplements
Rare mineral deposits carried to the surface by cryovolcanism
Subsurface ocean water with unique chemical properties
description: Elegy-Pale is a large ice world distinguished by the vast colonies of white ice algae that blanket its surface, giving the planet an ethereal, ghostly appearance. The algae thrive on the chemical energy from ammonia hot springs where the subsurface ocean breaches the ice shell, and have spread to cover nearly sixty percent of the surface in a living carpet of pale organic material.

The dense atmosphere traps enough heat to keep surface temperatures at the warmer end of the ice-world spectrum, and the ammonia content gives the air a sharp, eye-watering quality even through filtration equipment. The landscape is a study in white and pale blue — ice, snow, algae, and a sky of whitish haze that makes it difficult to distinguish ground from atmosphere. The effect is of a world fading into its own pallor.

The ice algae represent one of the most successful extremophile organisms ever documented, having colonized an entire planet from what began as small colonies around ammonia vents. Their spread has altered the planet's albedo and atmospheric chemistry, creating a feedback loop that maintains conditions favorable for their continued growth. In essence, the algae have terraformed their own world, albeit into conditions hostile to most other forms of life.

The algae biomass is edible and nutritious after processing, making Elegy-Pale a potential food source for the sector. Harvesting operations have begun on a trial basis, but the ecological implications of large-scale removal are unknown. The algae carpet stabilizes the ice shelves and moderates atmospheric chemistry, and removing too much could trigger a cascade of environmental changes. The planet serves as a cautionary example of how even simple life can become the keystone of a planetary system.
